course.name: Build With ESP32
course.about: From the first blink to a sensor node that sleeps on a battery: real labs on a real ESP32, each one checked by what the board itself says.

stages.name: First light
stages.builds: the board on USB, flashing a sketch, an LED and the serial monitor

checks.what: Blink the LED five times, the board saying so
Have the board say hello over serial

stages.name: Inputs
stages.builds: reading a button and an analog voltage

checks.what: Press the button three times, each counted once
Turn the pot end to end, the readings spreading at least 3000

stages.name: Sensors
stages.builds: a temperature and humidity sensor and a soil moisture sensor

checks.what: Read a room's temperature from the DHT22
Read dry and wet soil, the readings spreading at least 500

stages.name: Outputs
stages.builds: PWM brightness and switching a load with a relay

checks.what: Fade the LED up and down three times

stages.name: Connected
stages.builds: Wi-Fi and a little web server

checks.what: Join your Wi-Fi, the board saying its address
Answer a web request with a reading

stages.name: A real node
stages.builds: deep sleep, the start of a battery sensor node

checks.what: Wake from deep sleep three times

lab.title: Blink the LED
steps: Plug the board in with a data USB cable; MIA finds its serial port (the course page, or "which board is plugged in?").
Read the sketch: setup() runs once, loop() over and over; pinMode makes GPIO 2 an output.
Say "flash the blink lab" (or press Flash This Lab on the course page) and approve it: MIA builds it with PlatformIO and writes it to the board.
Watch the LED blink once a second, and the serial monitor count MIA BLINK 1, 2, 3.
Change delay(500) to delay(100), flash again, and see it blink faster.
lab.why: Every project starts here: proving the board, the cable, the upload and your code all work.
watch: A charge-only USB cable: the board lights but no port appears.
A board that won't take the upload: hold BOOT while it starts uploading.

steps.words: D2 (GPIO 2) to one end of the 220 ohm resistor
steps.why: The pin drives the LED through the resistor, which limits the current: without it the LED and the pin take far more than they should.

steps.words: the other end of the 220 ohm resistor to the LED's long leg (+)
steps.why: The LED's long leg (+) faces the pin: an LED passes current one way only.

steps.words: the LED's short leg (-) to GND
steps.why: The short leg (-) to ground closes the loop.

circuit.note: The onboard LED on GPIO 2 blinks too, with nothing wired: this build is your own LED on the same pin.

wiring: GPIO 2 (on most dev boards; else an LED and 220 ohm resistor from GPIO 2 to GND)
